nodes.name: Common reed
nodes.desc: A tall wetland grass that forms dense reedbeds along marsh edges and channels. Coypu and mallards are recorded feeding on it.

nodes.name: Narrow-leaf cattail
nodes.desc: A tall emergent marsh plant of shallow, still water that gives cover and food to waterbirds and fish.

nodes.name: Papyrus
nodes.desc: Thick papyrus swamp once dominated the Hula marsh, and a reintroduced stand grows in the reserve today.

nodes.name: Bermuda grass
nodes.desc: A creeping grass of damp meadows and field edges around the valley. Wild boar and mallards are recorded eating it.

nodes.name: Mallard
nodes.desc: A common dabbling duck of the open water and marsh edges. Recorded eating reed and Bermuda grass, and itself prey for jungle cats, otters and harriers.

nodes.name: Coypu
nodes.desc: A large semi-aquatic rodent from South America that now lives in the valley wetlands and eats reed and other water plants.

nodes.name: Carp and tilapia
nodes.desc: Fish of the lake and channels. Remains show that carp, tilapia and catfish lived in old Lake Hula, and pelicans and otters hunt fish here today.

nodes.name: Common crane
nodes.desc: Tens of thousands stop over in the valley each year on the flyway from Finland to Africa. It eats mostly plants and waste grain, with some animal food.

nodes.name: Wild boar
nodes.desc: An omnivore that roots in wet soil and eats plants, eggs and carrion. It is among the most recorded large mammals of the valley.

nodes.name: Mountain gazelle
nodes.desc: A small grazing antelope of the hills and open ground around the valley, and the most recorded mammal in this area.

nodes.name: Northern house mosquito
nodes.desc: Its larvae live in still water and feed on microbes and detritus, then the adults become food for frogs and other small predators.

nodes.name: Great white pelican
nodes.desc: Migrating flocks stop in Israel. They feed mainly on fish, often scooping them in groups in shallow water.

nodes.name: Marsh frog
nodes.desc: A large water frog of ponds and channels that preys on insects and small animals. It is eaten by cats, harriers, otters and jackals.

nodes.name: Western marsh harrier
nodes.desc: A raptor that hunts low over reedbeds for frogs and waterbirds.

nodes.name: Eurasian otter
nodes.desc: A semi-aquatic hunter of fish and frogs, recorded in the valley waterways.

nodes.name: Jungle cat
nodes.desc: The reed cat favours wetlands with dense reeds and hunts rodents, birds, frogs and fish.

nodes.name: Golden jackal
nodes.desc: An opportunistic hunter and scavenger of rodents, birds, frogs, reptiles, fruit and carrion. It is common in the valley.

nodes.name: Gray wolf
nodes.desc: Top predator of the region, hunting gazelle and boar. Wolves dominate jackals where they meet.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Warm, bright weather drives plant growth in the valley.

nodes.name: Springs and water level
nodes.desc: Perennial springs feed the marsh. Draining the old lake in the 1950s shows how much the web depends on water.

nodes.name: Peat soil
nodes.desc: Peat and wet soils form where the marsh stays flooded, and they dried and burned after drainage.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Microbes and invertebrates that break down dead reed and carcasses into nutrients.
